stem: Shortly after a red blood cell transfusion begins, a client develops chills, severe low-back pain, hypotension, and a sense of impending doom. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.A: Stop the transfusion immediately, maintain IV access with 0.9% saline, assess and support the client, and notify the blood bank and treating clinician per protocol.
options.B: Slow the transfusion, give an antipyretic, and continue the same unit while monitoring whether the chills and back pain improve.
options.C: Pause the transfusion, give an antihistamine, and restart the same unit when the symptoms begin to resolve.
options.D: Complete the current unit before notifying the blood bank because stopping early can interfere with identifying the cause of the reaction.

rationale: Current NCBI/StatPearls transfusion guidance states that a suspected transfusion reaction requires immediate cessation of the transfusion, maintenance of IV access, patient assessment, and notification of the clinician/blood bank. Acute hemolytic reactions can include chills, low-back pain and shock/hypotension. A is therefore the priority response; continuing or restarting the same unit is unsafe.
educational_objective: Immediately stop a suspected serious transfusion reaction, maintain IV access with compatible saline, assess/support the client, and activate the transfusion-reaction notification process.

source_original.stem: Shortly after a red blood cell transfusion begins, a client develops chills, severe low-back pain, hypotension, and a sense of impending doom. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.A: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep IV access open with 0.9% saline, assess and support the client, and notify the blood bank and treating clinician per protocol.
options.B: Slow the transfusion, give an antipyretic, and continue the same unit while monitoring whether the chills and back pain improve.
options.C: Pause the transfusion, give an antihistamine, and restart the same unit when the symptoms begin to resolve.
options.D: Complete the current unit before notifying the blood bank because stopping early can interfere with identifying the cause of the reaction.

source_original.rationale: Chills, severe back pain, hypotension, and impending-doom symptoms shortly after a transfusion raise concern for a serious acute transfusion reaction. The priority is to stop the blood product immediately, maintain IV access with normal saline, assess and support the client, and notify the blood bank and treating clinician according to the reaction protocol. Continuing or restarting the same unit is unsafe.
